key_terms.meaning: A = U − TS, with U internal energy, T absolute temperature, S entropy; natural variables T and V
G = H − TS = A + PV, with H enthalpy and P pressure; natural variables T and P
A change of independent variable made by subtracting a product of conjugate variables, e.g. TS or PV, from a potential
−ΔA is the maximum work at constant T and V; −ΔG is the maximum non-PV work at constant T and P
dU = TdS − PdV, dH = TdS + VdP, dA = −SdT − PdV, dG = −SdT + VdP
A differential whose mixed second partial derivatives are equal, so its value depends only on the end states
(∂(G/T)/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = −H/T², linking the temperature change of G to H
Four equalities such as (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>, obtained from exactness of the potentials
μ = (∂T/∂P)<sub>H</sub> = [T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − V]/Cp; positive μ means the gas cools on throttling
Mᴿ = M − M<sup>ig</sup>, the difference between a real-fluid property and its ideal-gas value at the same T and P
Another name for a residual property, usually written for H, S, G and V
x = mass of vapour ÷ total mass in a two-phase mixture, ranging from 0 to 1
The condition where liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium at a given P or T
dP<sup>sat</sup>/dT = ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/(T·ΔV), the slope of a saturation curve
Cp − Cv = −T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>² ÷ (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = Tvα²/κ<sub>T</sub>; equal to R for an ideal gas, never negative, and zero only when α = 0
γ = Cp/Cv, never below 1: 5/3 for a monatomic and about 1.40 for a diatomic ideal gas, about 1.01 for liquid water
κ = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub>, a positive PVT derivative used in many identities
Writing a partial derivative as ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y) so that chain rules and variable swaps follow algebraically

takeaways: Free energies exist because at fixed T and V, or fixed T and P, part of the internal energy is unavailable as work.
All thermodynamic relations for a pure fluid follow from just two statements: energy conservation and the entropy inequality.
Maxwell relations turn entropy derivatives, which cannot be measured, into P–V–T derivatives, which can.
A residual property carries an equation of state into H, S and G: the real value is the ideal-gas value plus the residual at the same T and P.
Inside the saturation dome every specific property is a straight-line mixture of saturated liquid and saturated vapour values, weighted by quality.
The Clausius–Clapeyron equation predicts how boiling point shifts with pressure, which is why a pressure cooker cooks faster.
Cp − Cv equals R for an ideal gas, about 1 J/(mol·K) for liquid water and more than R for a dense gas; it is never negative.
The Jacobian method removes guesswork: any partial derivative can be reduced to P, V, T, Cp and Cv by a fixed recipe.
bank_note: Long answers here are mostly derivations with a numerical check. Examiners reward the starting relation stated in full, each differentiation step with the variable held constant, and a final result in measurable P–V–T and heat-capacity terms, evaluated with numbers and units.

bank.q: State the four fundamental property relations for U, H, A and G. Explain what the natural variables of each potential are and why that pair is natural.
outline: dU = T dS − P dV from the two laws
dH, dA, dG from the definitions
Natural variables and the read-off identities
Why the pair is natural: complete information and the equilibrium test
answer: Take a closed, simple compressible system on a reversible path. The first law gives dU = δQ − δW; the second law gives δQ<sub>rev</sub> = T dS; the only work is P dV. So dU = T dS − P dV. Because U, S and V are properties, this holds between any two neighbouring equilibrium states, reversible path or not.
Definitions: H = U + PV, A = U − TS, G = H − TS. Units: U, H, A, G in J (J/mol per mole), T in K, S in J/K, P in Pa, V in m³.

answer.text: Differentiate each definition and substitute dU:
answer.pre:
dH = dU + P dV + V dP = T dS + V dP
dA = dU − T dS − S dT = −S dT − P dV
dG = dH − T dS − S dT = −S dT + V dP

answer.text: Natural variables and read-off identities (compare dz = M dx + N dy, where M = (∂z/∂x)<sub>y</sub>):

answer: Why these pairs are natural. (1) Complete information: if G is known as a function of T and P, every other property follows by differentiation: S = −(∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub>, V = (∂G/∂P)<sub>T</sub>, H = G + TS, U = H − PV. If G were known as a function of, say, T and V, that would not be true. (2) Each pair is produced by a Legendre transform: subtracting TS swaps S for T, adding PV swaps V for P.

(3) Equilibrium test: at fixed natural variables the potential is a minimum at equilibrium. U is least at fixed S and V, H at fixed S and P, A at fixed T and V, and G at fixed T and P. Since temperature and pressure are what a plant controls, G(T, P) is the potential of chemical engineering.

Numerical check of (∂G/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = V. One mole of ideal gas at 300 K, 1 → 5 bar: ΔG = ∫V dP = RT ln 5 = 8.314 × 300 × 1.6094 = 4014 J. Liquid water at 25 °C, 1 → 100 bar, V nearly constant: ΔG = VΔP = 18.07 × 10⁻⁶ × 99 × 10⁵ = 178.9 J/mol. The gas value is 22 times larger because its volume is about 1400 times larger at 1 bar.
Check of (∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = −S: S is positive above 0 K, so G falls as T rises, fastest for the gas, which is why heating eventually turns a liquid into vapour.
Conclusion: the four relations are one statement (dU = T dS − P dV) seen in four sets of variables. Choose the potential whose natural variables are the ones held fixed in the problem.

bank.q: Explain why the Helmholtz and Gibbs free energies are called Legendre transforms, and show that −ΔA is the maximum work at constant T and V while −ΔG is the maximum non-expansion work at constant T and P.
outline: Legendre transform: swap a variable for its conjugate
Second law for an isothermal process: Q ≤ TΔS
W ≤ −ΔA; non-PV work ≤ −ΔG
A numerical example such as a fuel cell
answer: A Legendre transform changes the independent variable of a function from x to its slope. U(S, V) has slopes T = (∂U/∂S)<sub>V</sub> and −P = (∂U/∂V)<sub>S</sub>. The new function A = U − TS has dA = −S dT − P dV, so its variables are T and V; G = U − TS + PV has variables T and P.
This matters because S cannot be set on a dial, while T and P can. The transform keeps all the information of U(S, V) but expresses it in controllable variables.

Maximum work at constant T. A closed system exchanges heat only with surroundings at T. The second law gives ΔS ≥ Q/T, so Q ≤ TΔS. The first law gives W = Q − ΔU, with W the total work done by the system.
Then W ≤ TΔS − ΔU = −(ΔU − TΔS) = −ΔA, because T is constant. The equality holds for a reversible change. So −ΔA is the largest total work, including any expansion work.

At constant T and P, split the work into expansion work PΔV and other work W′ (electrical, shaft or surface work): W = PΔV + W′. Then W′ ≤ −ΔA − PΔV = −(ΔU + PΔV − TΔS) = −ΔG. So −ΔG is the largest non-expansion work.
Example, a hydrogen fuel cell at 298.15 K and 1 bar: H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), with ΔH° = −285.8 kJ/mol and ΔG° = −237.1 kJ/mol. The largest electrical work is 237.1 kJ per mole of H₂.

The cell voltage follows from W′ = nFE: E = 237 100/(2 × 96 485) = 1.229 V. The ideal efficiency, electrical work over heat of combustion, is 237.1/285.8 = 0.830. The other 285.8 − 237.1 = 48.7 kJ must leave as heat even in a reversible cell, because the reaction lowers the entropy of the system by 48 700/298.15 = 163.3 J/K.
Second example, boiling water at 1 atm: ΔG = 0 because the phases are in equilibrium, so no non-expansion work is available; but ΔA = −PΔV = −3.05 kJ/mol, which is the expansion work of the steam.

Conclusion: A and G are U with the "unavailable" TS removed, written in the variables that are held fixed. Their decrease sets an upper bound on work, and a negative ΔG at fixed T and P is the test for a spontaneous change.

bank.q: Define a residual property and explain why the ideal-gas state at the same temperature and pressure is chosen as the reference rather than the ideal-gas state at the same temperature and volume.
outline: M<sup>R</sup> = M − M<sup>ig</sup> at the same T and P
Residuals vanish as P → 0 (except V<sup>R</sup> → B)
Ideal-gas part from Cp<sup>ig</sup> alone; residual from PVT data
G<sup>R</sup> = RT ln φ links to fugacity
answer: Definition: M<sup>R</sup>(T, P) = M(T, P) − M<sup>ig</sup>(T, P), where M is any molar property (V, U, H, S, A, G) of the real fluid and M<sup>ig</sup> is the value the fluid would have as an ideal gas at the same T and P.

Why the same T and P. A property is calculated as M = M<sup>ig</sup> + M<sup>R</sup>. The ideal-gas part needs only C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup>(T) and the ideal-gas laws: H<sup>ig</sup> depends on T alone and S<sup>ig</sup>(T, P) = S<sup>ig</sup>(T, P°) + ∫C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup> dT/T − R ln(P/P°). Temperature and pressure are what we measure and set in a plant, so the property is wanted at given T and P.
The residual then comes from an isothermal integral in pressure from P = 0, where every real gas is ideal, to the actual P:

answer.pre:
G<sup>R</sup>/RT = ∫₀<sup>P</sup> (Z − 1) dP/P
H<sup>R</sup> = ∫₀<sup>P</sup> [V − T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>] dP
S<sup>R</sup> = ∫₀<sup>P</sup> [R/P − (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>] dP

answer: These start from a clean lower limit, need only PVT data or an equation of state, and give G<sup>R</sup> = RT ln φ, which joins the residuals to fugacity and phase equilibrium.

Why not the same T and V. At a given T and V the real gas and the ideal gas have different pressures. The difference M − M<sup>ig</sup>(T, V) then mixes two effects: the real-gas deviation and the change of the ideal-gas property with pressure (for S and G an extra R ln Z term). It would not vanish neatly at low pressure in the same way and would not plug into the tables built at fixed P.

Limit behaviour: as P → 0, H<sup>R</sup>, S<sup>R</sup>, G<sup>R</sup>, U<sup>R</sup> and A<sup>R</sup> → 0. V<sup>R</sup> = (Z − 1)RT/P is the exception: it tends to the second virial coefficient B, because both V and V<sup>ig</sup> grow without limit while their difference stays finite.

Example, CO₂ at 350 K and 20 bar (virial equation with the Abbott correlation): Z = 0.9425, G<sup>R</sup> = −167.5 J/mol, H<sup>R</sup> = −598.4 J/mol and S<sup>R</sup> = −1.231 J/(mol·K). So the real enthalpy is 598.4 J/mol below the ideal-gas value at the same T and P.

Check: G<sup>R</sup> = H<sup>R</sup> − TS<sup>R</sup> = −598.4 + 350 × 1.231 = −167.5 J/mol, and φ = exp(−167.5/2909.9) = 0.944. Negative residuals at moderate pressure come from molecular attraction.

bank.q: Write the Clapeyron equation, derive it from the equality of Gibbs energy of two phases, state the assumptions used to obtain the integrated Clausius–Clapeyron form, and derive that form.
outline: dG equal for both phases along the curve
dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV = ΔH/(TΔV)
Assumptions: V<sub>l</sub> neglected, ideal vapour, constant ΔH
Integrated form and the ln P against 1/T line
answer: At a point on the coexistence curve two phases α and β of a pure substance are in equilibrium at the same T and P, so G<sup>α</sup> = G<sup>β</sup> (molar Gibbs energies).
Move a small step along the curve. Both phases stay in equilibrium, so dG<sup>α</sup> = dG<sup>β</sup>: −S<sup>α</sup> dT + V<sup>α</sup> dP = −S<sup>β</sup> dT + V<sup>β</sup> dP.

Rearranging: dP/dT = (S<sup>β</sup> − S<sup>α</sup>)/(V<sup>β</sup> − V<sup>α</sup>) = ΔS/ΔV. For a reversible phase change at fixed T, ΔS = ΔH/T. Hence the Clapeyron equation dP<sub>sat</sub>/dT = ΔH/(T ΔV). It is exact for a pure substance; no assumption has been made yet.

Example of the exact form, ice melting at 273.15 K: ΔH = 6010 J/mol, ΔV = 18.02 × 10⁻⁶ − 19.65 × 10⁻⁶ = −1.63 × 10⁻⁶ m³/mol, so dP/dT = 6010/(273.15 × −1.63 × 10⁻⁶) = −1.350 × 10⁷ Pa/K = −135 bar/K. The negative slope is why ice melts at a slightly lower temperature under pressure.

Assumptions for vaporisation: (1) far from the critical point V<sub>l</sub> ≪ V<sub>g</sub>, so ΔV ≈ V<sub>g</sub>; (2) the vapour is ideal, V<sub>g</sub> = RT/P; (3) ΔH<sub>vap</sub> is constant over the temperature range.

answer.pre:
dP/dT = ΔH P/(R T²)
dP/P = (ΔH/R) dT/T²
ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)
ln P = A − ΔH/(RT)

answer: So a plot of ln P<sub>sat</sub> against 1/T is a straight line of slope −ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R, and two points give ΔH<sub>vap</sub>.

Check of the ideal-vapour assumptions at 1 atm: the exact Clapeyron slope with the real ΔV = 0.03013 m³/mol is dP/dT = 40 650/(373.12 × 0.03013) = 3616 Pa/K, while the ideal-vapour form gives ΔH P/(RT²) = 40 650 × 101 325/(8.314 × 373.12²) = 3559 Pa/K, only 1.6 % lower. Units: J mol⁻¹ ÷ (K · m³ mol⁻¹) = Pa/K.

Check against steam tables: the true value is 41.7 kPa, so the estimate is 2.7 % high. The error comes mostly from assumption (3): ΔH<sub>vap</sub> of water rises from 40.65 kJ/mol at 373 K to 41.7 kJ/mol at 350 K. Near the critical point all three assumptions fail, and the exact Clapeyron form with real ΔV must be used.

bank.q: Using the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>, derive the internal-pressure expression (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> − P. Evaluate it for a gas obeying P(V − b) = RT and for a van der Waals gas, with numbers for CO₂ at 300 K and V = 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³/mol.
outline: Divide dU = T dS − P dV by dV at constant T
Substitute the Maxwell relation from dA
P(V − b) = RT gives zero
van der Waals gives a/V²; numbers and meaning
answer: Start from the fundamental relation dU = T dS − P dV. Divide by dV holding T constant: (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> − P.
The entropy slope cannot be measured directly. From dA = −S dT − P dV, exactness gives the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>.
Substituting: (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> − P. This is the internal pressure, the energy change per unit volume at fixed temperature. It needs only the equation of state.
Gas obeying P(V − b) = RT: P = RT/(V − b), so (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = R/(V − b) and T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = RT/(V − b) = P. Therefore (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = P − P = 0.

Meaning: this gas has a finite molecular volume b but no attraction. Moving the molecules apart costs no energy, so U depends on T only, exactly as for an ideal gas, even though the gas is not ideal (Z = PV/RT = 1 + bP/RT > 1). Zero internal pressure is a statement about attraction, not about ideality.
van der Waals gas: P = RT/(V − b) − a/V². (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = R/(V − b), so T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> − P = RT/(V − b) − RT/(V − b) + a/V² = a/V².
Numbers for CO₂ (a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻², b = 4.267 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol) at 300 K and V = 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³/mol: (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = 0.364/(1.00 × 10⁻³)² = 3.64 × 10⁵ Pa = 364 kPa.

The pressure itself is P = 8.314 × 300/0.00095733 − 364 000 = 2 605 400 − 364 000 = 2.241 × 10⁶ Pa, so the internal pressure is 364/2241 = 0.162 of the external pressure: a sixth of the push on the walls is offset by attraction.
Integrating at 300 K from 1.00 × 10⁻³ to 1.00 × 10⁻² m³/mol: ΔU = a(1/V₁ − 1/V₂) = 0.364 × 900 = 327.6 J/mol, the energy needed to pull the molecules apart.

head: Model
(∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub>
Value for CO₂ at V = 10⁻³ m³/mol

answer: Consequence, a free (Joule) expansion into vacuum: Q = 0 and W = 0, so ΔU = 0. For the van der Waals gas this means C<sub>V</sub> ΔT = −a(1/V₁ − 1/V₂) = −327.6 J/mol; with C<sub>V</sub> = 28.9 J/(mol·K) for CO₂ the gas cools by 327.6/28.9 = 11.3 K. An ideal gas, or a P(V − b) = RT gas, would not change temperature at all.
Check of units: Pa = J/m³, so (∂U/∂V)<sub>T</sub> in Pa is J per m³ of volume change, consistent with ΔU in J/mol.

bank.q: Derive the general relation Cp − Cv = −T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>² ÷ (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> and show its value for an ideal gas and for a van der Waals gas (CO₂ at 300 K and V = 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³/mol).
outline: Write S(T, V) and differentiate at constant P
Maxwell relation and the cyclic relation
Ideal gas gives R
van der Waals numbers and comparison with R
answer: Take S as a function of T and V: dS = (∂S/∂T)<sub>V</sub> dT + (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> dV, with (∂S/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = C<sub>V</sub>/T.

Divide by dT at constant P: (∂S/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = C<sub>V</sub>/T + (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>. The left side is C<sub>P</sub>/T, so C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = T(∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>.
Maxwell relation from dA: (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>. So C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>.

Cyclic relation: (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = −(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>/(∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>. Substituting gives C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = −T(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>²/(∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>. With α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> and κ<sub>T</sub> = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub> this is also C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = TVα²/κ<sub>T</sub>.

Sign: (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> < 0 for every stable phase, and the square is positive, so C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> ≥ 0, with equality only when (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = 0, that is α = 0 (water near 4 °C).
Ideal gas: P = RT/V, so (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = R/V and (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = −RT/V². Then C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = −T(R/V)²/(−RT/V²) = R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

answer.text: van der Waals gas: (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = R/(V − b) and (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = −RT/(V − b)² + 2a/V³. For CO₂ (a = 0.364, b = 4.267 × 10⁻⁵) at 300 K and V = 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³/mol:

answer: So C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = 11.35/8.314 = 1.37 R. Attraction makes the gas easier to compress (the +2a/V³ term shrinks the size of (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>), so the expansion at constant pressure is larger and needs more heat than for an ideal gas.

Check: an accurate equation of state for CO₂ at this state (22.4 bar) gives C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub> = 14.6 J/(mol·K); the van der Waals result has the right direction and about three quarters of the size.
Check of the α, κ<sub>T</sub> form for an ideal gas: α = 1/T and κ<sub>T</sub> = 1/P, so TVα²/κ<sub>T</sub> = TV(1/T²)P = PV/T = R, the same result.

Why the relation is useful: C<sub>V</sub> of a liquid or solid is very hard to measure, because holding the volume fixed while heating needs enormous pressures. Engineers measure C<sub>P</sub> and compute C<sub>V</sub> from α and κ<sub>T</sub>.

Near the critical point (∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> → 0, so C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>V</sub>, and C<sub>P</sub> itself, grow very large; at the critical point C<sub>P</sub> is infinite. For a liquid such as water at 300 K the same formula gives only 0.91 J/(mol·K).

bank.q: Use the Jacobian method to express (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> in terms of measurable quantities, stating each rule used. Evaluate it for liquid water at 25 °C and for nitrogen gas at 300 K and low pressure, and relate it to the Joule–Thomson coefficient.
outline: dH = T dS + V dP gives (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> + V
(∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = J(S, T)/J(P, T), expanded in (T, V)
Maxwell and cyclic relations give V − T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>
Numbers for water and N₂; (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −C<sub>P</sub> μ<sub>JT</sub>
answer: Rule 1, the fundamental relation: dH = T dS + V dP. Divide by dP at constant T: (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> + V. Only the entropy slope remains to be expressed.
Rule 2, the key identity: a partial derivative is a ratio of Jacobians with the held variable in both, (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = J(S, T)/J(P, T).

Rule 3, expand both Jacobians in one pair, here (T, V): J(S, T) = (∂S/∂T)<sub>V</sub>(∂T/∂V)<sub>T</sub> − (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub>(∂T/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = −(∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub>, and in the same way J(P, T) = −(∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>. So (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub>/(∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub>.
Rule 4, Maxwell relation from dA: (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>. Rule 5, cyclic relation: (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>/(∂P/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>.

Result: (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = V − T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = V(1 − Tα). Ideal gas check: T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = RT/P = V, so (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = 0; the enthalpy of an ideal gas does not depend on pressure.

Liquid water at 25 °C (V = 18.07 × 10⁻⁶ m³/mol, α = 2.573 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹): (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = 18.07 × 10⁻⁶ × (1 − 0.0767) = 1.668 × 10⁻⁵ J/(mol·Pa). From 1 to 100 bar, ΔH = 165.2 J/mol (tables: 164.5 J/mol).

Nitrogen at 300 K, low pressure, virial V = RT/P + B: (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = R/P + dB/dT, so (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = B − T dB/dT. The Abbott correlation (T<sub>c</sub> = 126.2 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 34.0 bar, ω = 0.038) gives B = −5.39 cm³/mol and T dB/dT = 52.34 cm³/mol, so (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −57.7 cm³/mol = −5.77 J/(mol·bar).

Joule–Thomson link, by the cyclic relation on H, T, P: (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂H/∂T)<sub>P</sub>(∂T/∂P)<sub>H</sub> = −C<sub>P</sub> μ<sub>JT</sub>. So μ<sub>JT</sub> = [T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − V]/C<sub>P</sub>.

Application: throttling nitrogen at 300 K from 100 bar to 1 bar gives roughly ΔT ≈ μ<sub>JT</sub> ΔP = 0.198 × (−99) = −19.6 K. This is only an estimate, because μ<sub>JT</sub> changes along the throttle; integrating along the isenthalp with accurate data gives a drop of the same size.
Check: an accurate equation of state gives μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0.212 K/bar for nitrogen at 300 K and 1 bar, within 7 % of the virial estimate; a 100 bar throttle cools nitrogen by roughly 20 K.

bank.q: Steam at 0.5 MPa has a quality of 0.85. Using saturated-steam table values, calculate its temperature, specific volume, specific enthalpy, specific entropy and specific internal energy, and state the assumptions used.
outline: Saturated values at 0.5 MPa
M = M<sub>f</sub> + x(M<sub>g</sub> − M<sub>f</sub>) for v, h, s
u from h − Pv as a check
Each result lies between the liquid and vapour values
answer: The state is a wet mixture because 0 < x < 1, so the temperature is the saturation temperature, 151.8 °C; T and P are not weighted by quality.
Specific enthalpy: h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>fg</sub> = 640.19 + 0.85 × 2107.92 = 640.19 + 1791.73 = 2431.9 kJ/kg.
Specific entropy: s = s<sub>f</sub> + x s<sub>fg</sub> = 1.8606 + 0.85 × 4.9600 = 1.8606 + 4.2160 = 6.0766 kJ/(kg·K).

Specific internal energy: u = h − Pv = 2431.9 − 500 × 0.3187 = 2431.9 − 159.4 = 2272.5 kJ/kg (P in kPa times v in m³/kg gives kJ/kg). Using u<sub>f</sub> = 639.6 and u<sub>g</sub> = 2560.7 kJ/kg gives u = 639.6 + 0.85 × 1921.1 = 2272.5 kJ/kg, the same.

Assumptions: the mixture is in equilibrium, so both phases are at the same T and P; the liquid and vapour are each exactly saturated; the quality is a mass fraction, uniform over the sample; kinetic and potential energy are ignored.

Checks: each mixture value lies between the f and g values. Most of the volume is vapour even at x = 0.85: the liquid fills only 0.15 × 0.001093/0.3187 = 0.05 % of the space. Volume fraction and mass fraction are very different, which is why quality must not be read as a volume fraction.
Check: IAPWS-IF97 evaluated directly at 0.5 MPa and x = 0.85 gives v = 0.3187 m³/kg, h = 2431.9 kJ/kg, s = 6.0766 kJ/(kg·K) and u = 2272.5 kJ/kg, the same values.
Sketch: a T–s diagram with the dome, the horizontal 0.5 MPa line at 151.8 °C from s<sub>f</sub> = 1.861 to s<sub>g</sub> = 6.821, and the state marked 85 % of the way across, at s = 6.077 kJ/(kg·K).
Common errors: h = h<sub>f</sub> + x h<sub>g</sub> gives 640.19 + 0.85 × 2748.11 = 2976.1 kJ/kg, 544 kJ/kg too high; taking h = h<sub>g</sub> gives 2748.1, 316 kJ/kg too high.

bank.q: Vapour-pressure data for a pure liquid give a straight line of ln P<sub>sat</sub> against 1/T with slope −4200 K. The liquid boils at 350 K at 1 atm. Estimate the latent heat of vaporisation and the vapour pressure at 330 K, and explain the assumptions behind the estimate.
outline: Slope = −ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R
ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 4200 × 8.314
Integrated form for P at 330 K
Assumptions and what a curved plot means
answer: The integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation is ln P<sub>sat</sub> = A − ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/(RT), a straight line in 1/T with slope −ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R.
Latent heat: ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = −R × slope = 8.314 × 4200 = 34 919 J/mol = 34.9 kJ/mol. The slope is in kelvin because 1/T is in K⁻¹ and ln P has no units; R in J/(mol·K) then gives J/mol.

Trouton check: ΔS<sub>vap</sub> = ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/T<sub>b</sub> = 34 919/350 = 99.8 J/(mol·K). Trouton's rule gives about 85–88 J/(mol·K) for non-polar liquids, so this liquid is probably polar or hydrogen-bonded (water gives 109 J/(mol·K)).

Assumptions: (1) the vapour is an ideal gas, V<sub>g</sub> = RT/P; (2) the liquid volume is negligible, ΔV ≈ V<sub>g</sub>; (3) ΔH<sub>vap</sub> is constant over the range of the data; (4) the liquid and vapour are pure, so the measured pressure is the saturation pressure.

The estimate is therefore an average ΔH<sub>vap</sub> over the temperature range of the data. Real latent heats fall as temperature rises and vanish at the critical point, so a plot over a wide range curves slightly, with its magnitude of slope decreasing at high T (small 1/T).
When the plot curves, fit the Antoine equation ln P = A − B/(T + C) instead, and take ΔH<sub>vap</sub> at a given T from the local slope: ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = RB T²/(T + C)².
Back-substitution check at 350 K: ln P = 23.526 − 4200/350 = 23.526 − 12.000 = 11.526, so P = e<sup>11.526</sup> = 101 325 Pa, the given boiling point.
Sketch: ln P against 1/T, a straight line falling from left to right with slope −4200 K, passing through (1/350, 11.526) and (1/330, 10.799).
Conclusion: ΔH<sub>vap</sub> ≈ 34.9 kJ/mol and P<sub>sat</sub>(330 K) ≈ 49.0 kPa, reliable to a few per cent at pressures up to a few bar.

bank.q: Starting from the residual Gibbs energy, find the fugacity coefficient of a pure gas from the van der Waals equation. Work it for CO₂ at 350 K and 20 bar (a = 0.364 Pa m⁶ mol⁻², b = 4.267 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol), and check the result.
outline: ln φ = G<sup>R</sup>/RT = ∫₀<sup>P</sup> (Z − 1) dP/P
vdW in Z form: Z³ − (1 + B)Z² + AZ − AB = 0
ln φ = Z − 1 − ln(Z − B) − A/Z
Checks: φ → 1 as P → 0; compare with the virial result
answer: Definition: ln φ = G<sup>R</sup>/RT = ∫₀<sup>P</sup> (Z − 1) dP/P at constant T. Because the van der Waals equation is explicit in P, change the variable to V (or Z); the integral then closes in terms of Z.
Dimensionless parameters: A = aP/(RT)² and B = bP/(RT). The equation P = RT/(V − b) − a/V² becomes the cubic Z³ − (1 + B)Z² + AZ − AB = 0.

Integrating the residual Gibbs energy for this equation gives the standard result ln φ = Z − 1 − ln(Z − B) − A/Z. The term −ln(Z − B) comes from repulsion (raises φ), the term −A/Z from attraction (lowers φ).
Solve the cubic Z³ − 1.02933Z² + 0.08598Z − 0.002521 = 0 for the vapour root (start at Z = 1 and iterate): Z = 0.9408. Molar volume V = ZRT/P = 0.9408 × 2909.9/2.0 × 10⁶ = 1.369 × 10⁻³ m³/mol.
Check 1, low-pressure limit: as P → 0, A and B → 0 and Z → 1, so ln φ → 0 − ln 1 − 0 = 0 and φ → 1, as required for an ideal gas.

Check 2, other methods at the same state: the virial equation with the Abbott correlation gives φ = 0.944, and an accurate equation of state for CO₂ gives 0.9436. All three agree to 0.1 %, because 20 bar is a modest pressure for CO₂ at 350 K (P<sub>r</sub> = 0.27).

Use: at vapour–liquid equilibrium the same equation gives a liquid root and a vapour root, and the saturation pressure is the P at which φ<sub>l</sub> = φ<sub>v</sub>. H<sup>R</sup> and S<sup>R</sup> follow from related integrals of the same equation, for example H<sup>R</sup> = RT(Z − 1) − a/V for van der Waals.

bank.q: Show from the Gibbs energy that (∂Cp/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −T(∂²V/∂T²)<sub>P</sub>, and use it with the virial equation to judge whether the heat capacity of CO₂ at 350 K can be treated as a function of temperature alone at 1 bar and at 20 bar.
outline: Maxwell relation from dG, then differentiate with respect to T
Cp = T(∂S/∂T)<sub>P</sub> and the order of differentiation
Virial: Cp − Cp<sup>ig</sup> = −TP d²B/dT²
Judge the size at 1 bar and 20 bar
answer: From dG = −S dT + V dP, exactness gives the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>.

C<sub>P</sub> = T(∂S/∂T)<sub>P</sub>, so (∂C<sub>P</sub>/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = T ∂/∂P[(∂S/∂T)<sub>P</sub>]<sub>T</sub> = T ∂/∂T[(∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub>]<sub>P</sub>, because the order of mixed second derivatives of the state function S(T, P) does not matter.
Substituting the Maxwell relation: (∂C<sub>P</sub>/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = T ∂/∂T[−(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>]<sub>P</sub> = −T(∂²V/∂T²)<sub>P</sub>.
Ideal gas: V = RT/P, (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = R/P, (∂²V/∂T²)<sub>P</sub> = 0. So C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup> depends on T only.
Virial gas: V = RT/P + B(T), so (∂²V/∂T²)<sub>P</sub> = d²B/dT² and (∂C<sub>P</sub>/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −T d²B/dT². Integrating from P = 0: C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup> = −TP d²B/dT².

With the Abbott correlation, d²B/dT² = (R/(P<sub>c</sub> T<sub>c</sub>))(d²B⁰/dT<sub>r</sub>² + ω d²B¹/dT<sub>r</sub>²), where d²B⁰/dT<sub>r</sub>² = −1.755/T<sub>r</sub><sup>3.6</sup> and d²B¹/dT<sub>r</sub>² = −3.754/T<sub>r</sub><sup>6.2</sup>. For CO₂ at 350 K (T<sub>r</sub> = 1.1506, ω = 0.224): d²B/dT² = −5.226 × 10⁻⁹ m³ mol⁻¹ K⁻².

answer.text: Size of the correction (C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup> of CO₂ at 350 K = 39.39 J/(mol·K)):

answer: Check: an accurate equation of state gives C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup> = 3.96 J/(mol·K) at 20 bar, so the virial estimate is within 8 % of the correction itself.

Judgement: at 1 bar the pressure effect (0.5 %) is below the uncertainty of most C<sub>P</sub> data, so C<sub>P</sub> = C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup>(T) is fine. At 20 bar it is 9 %, too large to ignore in an energy balance; and near the critical point (T<sub>r</sub> → 1, P<sub>r</sub> → 1) d²V/dT² grows sharply and C<sub>P</sub> rises steeply.

Consistency with residual enthalpy: since C<sub>P</sub> = (∂H/∂T)<sub>P</sub>, C<sub>P</sub> − C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup> = (∂H<sup>R</sup>/∂T)<sub>P</sub>. With H<sup>R</sup> = P(B − T dB/dT), (∂H<sup>R</sup>/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = P(dB/dT − dB/dT − T d²B/dT²) = −PT d²B/dT², exactly the same expression, so the two routes agree.
Sketch: C<sub>P</sub> against P at 350 K, a horizontal line at C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup> = 39.39 for an ideal gas and a rising line for CO₂ reaching about 43 J/(mol·K) at 20 bar.

Practical rule: treat C<sub>P</sub> as a function of T alone for gases at reduced pressures below about 0.05; above that, use C<sub>P</sub><sup>ig</sup>(T) for the ideal-gas path and add the pressure effect through residual enthalpy, which carries the same information.

bank.q: Propane at 360 K and 15 bar flows to a compressor. Using the virial equation with the Abbott correlation (T<sub>c</sub> = 369.8 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 42.48 bar, ω = 0.152), find Z, φ, G<sup>R</sup>, H<sup>R</sup> and S<sup>R</sup>. Compare with accurate values (Z = 0.854, H<sup>R</sup> = −1419 J/mol, S<sup>R</sup> = −2.80 J/(mol·K)) and analyse whether the correlation is adequate here.
outline: Reduced state and B⁰, B¹
Z, ln φ, G<sup>R</sup>
H<sup>R</sup> and S<sup>R</sup> from dB/dT<sub>r</sub> terms
Compare and judge the range of the two-term virial equation
answer: Reduced state: T<sub>r</sub> = 360/369.8 = 0.9735; P<sub>r</sub> = 15/42.48 = 0.3531. The gas is just below its critical temperature; its vapour pressure at 360 K is about 35.5 bar, so at 15 bar it is a vapour.
Slopes: dB⁰/dT<sub>r</sub> = 0.675/T<sub>r</sub><sup>2.6</sup> = 0.7238; dB¹/dT<sub>r</sub> = 0.722/T<sub>r</sub><sup>5.2</sup> = 0.8302.

S<sup>R</sup>/R = −P<sub>r</sub>(dB⁰/dT<sub>r</sub> + ω dB¹/dT<sub>r</sub>) = −0.3531 × (0.7238 + 0.1262) = −0.3001, so S<sup>R</sup> = −2.495 J/(mol·K). Check: H<sup>R</sup> − TS<sup>R</sup> = −1295.3 + 360 × 2.495 = −397.0 J/mol = G<sup>R</sup>.

Analysis: Z and φ, which depend on B itself, are good to 1.5 %. H<sup>R</sup> and S<sup>R</sup> depend on dB/dT, which a two-term fit reproduces less well, and the two-term virial equation omits the C/V² term that matters as the gas approaches saturation (here P/P<sub>sat</sub> ≈ 0.4 at T<sub>r</sub> < 1).

Judgement: the usual guide is that the two-term virial form is reliable when the reduced volume V<sub>r</sub> = V/V<sub>c</sub> is above about 2. Here V = ZRT/P = 1.704 × 10⁻³ m³/mol and V<sub>c</sub> = 200 cm³/mol, so V<sub>r</sub> = 8.5: Z is safely inside the range, but the enthalpy is already 9 % off because T<sub>r</sub> is close to 1. For a compressor power estimate, an error of 124 J/mol in H<sup>R</sup> against a compression work of a few kJ/mol is a few per cent and usually acceptable; for a design close to saturation, use a cubic equation of state (Peng–Robinson) or the Lee–Kesler tables instead.

bank.q: Derive the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation from the fundamental relation for G, use it to obtain the temperature dependence of the equilibrium constant, and evaluate what it says about ammonia synthesis between 298 K and 700 K.
outline: Quotient rule on G/T with (∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = −S
ΔG° = −RT ln K gives d ln K/dT = ΔH°/RT²
Integrate with constant ΔH°
Ammonia numbers and the plant compromise
answer: From dG = −S dT + V dP, (∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = −S. Differentiate G/T by the quotient rule: [∂(G/T)/∂T]<sub>P</sub> = (1/T)(∂G/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − G/T² = −S/T − G/T² = −(G + TS)/T².
Since G + TS = H, this is the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation: [∂(G/T)/∂T]<sub>P</sub> = −H/T². It holds for each species, and so for a reaction: d(ΔG°/T)/dT = −ΔH°/T².
With ΔG° = −RT ln K, ΔG°/T = −R ln K, so −R d ln K/dT = −ΔH°/T², which gives the van 't Hoff equation d ln K/dT = ΔH°/(RT²).
For constant ΔH°: ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). An exothermic reaction (ΔH° < 0) has K falling as T rises; an endothermic one has K rising.
Ammonia: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ with ΔH°₂₉₈ = 2 × (−45.9) = −91.8 kJ and ΔG°₂₉₈ = 2 × (−16.4) = −32.8 kJ.

answer.text: K at higher temperature, ΔH° taken as constant (ΔH°/R = −11 042 K):

answer: Check on the sign: ΔS° = (ΔH° − ΔG°)/T = (−91 800 + 32 800)/298.15 = −197.9 J/K; four moles of gas become two, so the entropy falls and the −TΔS° term turns ΔG° positive above about 91 800/197.9 = 464 K.

Evaluation: equilibrium favours ammonia at low temperature, but the reaction is far too slow there even on an iron catalyst. Plants therefore run at about 400–500 °C for rate, accept the small K, and push the equilibrium back with high pressure (150–300 bar), because Le Chatelier's principle favours the side with fewer moles of gas, and they recycle unreacted gas.
Check at 700 K: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −8.314 × 700 × (−8.03) = +46.7 kJ, and directly ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −91.8 + 700 × 0.1979 = +46.7 kJ. The two agree because both assume constant ΔH° and ΔS°.

Limits of the estimate: ΔH° of ammonia synthesis becomes somewhat more negative at high temperature, so the constant-ΔH° values are rough; a careful calculation integrates ΔC<sub>P</sub>° as well. The direction and the order of magnitude of the fall in K are what the equation reliably tells the designer.

bank.q: Using the Jacobian method and a Maxwell relation, derive an expression for the Joule–Thomson coefficient in terms of P–V–T data and Cp. Evaluate it for nitrogen and hydrogen at 300 K with the virial equation, and judge why hydrogen must be pre-cooled before throttling in a liquefaction plant.
outline: μ<sub>JT</sub> = J(T, H)/J(P, H) expanded in (T, P)
Maxwell relation gives μ = [T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − V]/Cp
Virial form μ = (T dB/dT − B)/Cp with numbers
Inversion temperature and the pre-cooling decision
answer: Target: μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T/∂P)<sub>H</sub> = J(T, H)/J(P, H).

Expand in (T, P). Numerator: J(T, H) = (∂T/∂T)<sub>P</sub>(∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> − (∂T/∂P)<sub>T</sub>(∂H/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub>. Denominator: J(P, H) = (∂P/∂T)<sub>P</sub>(∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> − (∂P/∂P)<sub>T</sub>(∂H/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = −C<sub>P</sub>.

So μ<sub>JT</sub> = −(∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub>/C<sub>P</sub>. From dH = T dS + V dP and the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>: (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = V − T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>. Hence μ<sub>JT</sub> = [T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − V]/C<sub>P</sub>.
Ideal gas: T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = RT/P = V, so μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0 and an ideal gas neither cools nor warms on throttling.
Virial gas, V = RT/P + B(T): T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − V = T dB/dT − B, so μ<sub>JT</sub> = (T dB/dT − B)/C<sub>P</sub> at low pressure. Cooling needs T dB/dT > B.

answer.text: Numbers at 300 K from the Abbott correlation:

answer: Working for hydrogen: μ<sub>JT</sub> = (4.19 − 8.52) × 10⁻⁶ m³/mol ÷ 28.85 J/(mol·K) = −1.50 × 10⁻⁷ K/Pa = −0.015 K/bar. Accurate data give +0.212 K/bar for N₂ and −0.030 K/bar for H₂, so the correlation has the right signs and sizes.

Inversion temperature: μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0 where T dB/dT = B. Solving with the Abbott correlation for hydrogen gives about 220 K at low pressure; accurate data put it near 200 K. Nitrogen's is above 600 K, so nitrogen cools when throttled from room temperature.

Why: at 300 K hydrogen molecules are so light and weakly attracting that repulsion dominates (B > 0); throttling then raises the temperature. Above the inversion temperature a Linde valve would heat the stream and no liquid could form.

At higher pressure the virial form is not enough: μ<sub>JT</sub> then depends on P as well, and the full inversion curve on a T–P diagram is a dome. Inside the dome throttling cools; outside it warms. For hydrogen the whole dome lies below about 200 K.
Sketch: a T–P diagram with curved isenthalps rising to a maximum and the inversion curve through those maxima; mark 300 K above the hydrogen dome and 77 K inside it.

Judgement: a hydrogen liquefier must first cool the gas well below 200 K, in practice with liquid nitrogen at 77 K, where μ<sub>JT</sub> for hydrogen is positive and large enough for the Linde cycle to work. Helium (inversion about 40 K) needs pre-cooling by liquid hydrogen or an expansion engine for the same reason. Pre-cooling costs energy but is unavoidable: without it the throttle works against liquefaction.

glossary.def: A property independent of the size of the system, such as temperature, pressure or molar volume.
A property that scales with the amount of material, such as total volume, internal energy or entropy.
A property whose change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken.
A differential expression whose integral between two states is path independent.
The partial molar Gibbs free energy, equal to (∂G/∂n<sub>i</sub>) at constant T, P and other mole numbers.
An effective pressure that replaces the true pressure in the ideal-gas chemical-potential formula, so that real-fluid behaviour is retained.
The ratio φ = f/P, tending to 1 as pressure tends to zero.
Z = PV/(RT); equal to 1 for an ideal gas and different from 1 for a real gas.
A relation among P, V and T for a fluid, such as the ideal-gas, van der Waals or Peng–Robinson equation.
Liquid at its boiling point for the given pressure, with quality zero.
Vapour at its condensation point for the given pressure, with quality one.
Vapour at a temperature above its saturation temperature for the given pressure.
Liquid at a temperature below its saturation temperature for the given pressure.
Enthalpy change when unit mass changes from saturated liquid to saturated vapour at constant temperature and pressure.
The single temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium.
The highest temperature and pressure at which liquid and vapour can be distinguished; above it there is one fluid phase.
A plot such as a T–s, P–h or Mollier diagram from which properties can be read graphically.
The temperature below which a gas cools on isenthalpic throttling and above which it warms.
The identity (∂x/∂y)<sub>z</sub> (∂y/∂z)<sub>x</sub> (∂z/∂x)<sub>y</sub> = −1 for three variables linked by a state relation.
κ = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub>, a positive quantity measuring volume change under pressure at fixed temperature.
α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>, the fractional volume change per kelvin at constant pressure.
A property divided by its critical value, such as T<sub>r</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub>, used in generalized correlations.
The principle that fluids at the same reduced temperature and reduced pressure have similar properties.
